To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the effects of repeated exposure to alcohol portrayals in TV fiction on self-reported alcohol use attitudes are (2) moderated by speed and (3) mediated by gut feelings.

the effects of repeated media exposure on self-reported evaluations are (a) moderated (i.e., stronger for those who are faster in expressing their gut feelings than for those who are slower) and (b) fully mediated (i.e., explained by the responses to self-repots tapping into gut feelings) by responses to self-report measures tapping into gut feelings, thus corroborating the logic of the cultivation hypothesis.
the relationship between fiction viewing and self-reported alcohol evaluations is moderated by speed of responding to self-reports and mediated by self-reports that measure gut feelings.

the cultivation hypothesis, as we have reconceptualized it here, predicts the effects of repeated media exposure to occur at the gut level of evaluations.
